reasoning_summary: Step 0003: DNF-SAT is indeed in L: a DNF string is satisfiable iff some disjunct (conjunct of literals) contains no complementary pair, and scanning terms/literal pairs with a constant number of pointers is logspace; syntactic well-formedness of the DNF string is also logspace-checkable. The phrase 'satisfy the first disjunct' is loose (the first disjunct may be internally contradictory, so one must find a consistent disjunct), but the claimed conclusion DNF-SAT in L is correct. The conditional 'if it is NP-complete then L=NP' is correct under the logspace many-one reductions the answer commits to later: NP logspace-reduces to a language in L, and L is closed under logspace many-one reductions, so NP subset of L. Step 0005: the main claim is correct; if L=NP then any B in NP is decidable in logspace, and since DNF-SAT is nontrivial (it has both yes-instances, e.g. x, and no-instances, e.g. x AND NOT x, or non-DNF strings), the logspace decider can map to a fixed yes/no instance, giving a logspace many-one reduction. The parenthetical 'every problem in NP is NP-complete under logspace reductions' is literally an overstatement, since trivial languages (empty set, Sigma*) are never many-one complete; but it is an aside not used anywhere in the argument, and the load-bearing instance (DNF-SAT) is nontrivial. Step 0007: the equivalence follows from the two conditionals in 0003 and 0005. Step 0009: correct - P != NP implies L != NP (L subset of P, and L=NP would force P=NP), so L != NP is a weaker hypothesis; and since 0007 makes L != NP equivalent to the desired conclusion, it is trivially the weakest sufficient hypothesis. No step fails.
